name: Yazi
version_context: Official sxyazi/yazi release ref v0.3.3 resolved to commit 7c445cef1fd9ff9d41314d3d2b02cbc74250c6bf; historical source snapshot, not a claim about the latest release.
summary: A Rust terminal file manager that separates queued background file work, cancellable previews, and Lua extension execution from interactive navigation.
scope: Task scheduling and progress at the v0.3.3 source boundary
Per-tab preview lifecycle and directory preview loading
Lua preview execution and synchronization with application state
Benefits and costs are architectural inferences, not benchmark results or security guarantees

features.name: Priority-queued background work
features.description: Scheduler::serve creates unbounded priority channels for micro and macro work, a progress channel, and configurable worker counts. Macro workers select between micro futures and file/plugin/prework operations; operations whose task ID is no longer ongoing are skipped. Cancellation can enqueue a cleanup hook or remove the ongoing task entry.
benefits: File operations and preparation work can progress independently of navigation
Task identifiers connect queued work, cancellation, and progress reporting
costs: Configured worker counts do not bound the memory consumed by unbounded queues
Cancellation and completion must coordinate through shared ongoing state; cancellation is not rollback of filesystem effects

features.name: Cancellable preview state
features.description: Preview::go checks a lock containing URL, skip offset, and file characteristics before reusing content, selects a previewer by URL/MIME, and cancels the previous preview before starting replacement work. Directory previews use a separately abortable loader and emit ticketed partial results in chunks capped at 50,000 entries or 500 milliseconds.
benefits: Incremental directory delivery lets preview results arrive before the full directory stream completes
costs: Metadata-based reuse is not a filesystem snapshot or a content-hash guarantee
Cancellation tokens, loader handles, and preview locks create multiple lifecycle states to coordinate

features.name: Separate Lua execution with application callbacks
features.description: Asynchronous peek runs on spawn_blocking with a slim Lua instance, cancellation-aware instruction hooks, and a cancellation-select boundary. Synchronous peek is dispatched to the application layer. For isolated Lua execution, ya.sync converts arguments to sendable data, emits an application callback, and awaits a one-shot reply.
benefits: Preview plugin execution can occur outside the shared application Lua context
Explicit callbacks provide a controlled synchronization point for shared plugin state
costs: Values crossing the callback boundary must satisfy the sendable conversion contract
Synchronous callbacks can delay application work; separate Lua contexts do not establish an operating-system security sandbox

mathematical_views.model: Priority queues with task-identity lifecycle transitions
mathematical_views.question: How does a navigation request become queued work, a running operation, progress, or cancellation?
assumptions: Represent state as micro queue, macro queue, ongoing task map, and worker states; enqueue, dequeue, progress, and cancel are transitions
Worker counts are finite, but queue capacity is unbounded in the inspected implementation
Removal from the ongoing map suppresses later dispatch checks; already performed I/O is not reversed
No fairness, latency bound, or memory bound follows without workload and scheduler assumptions

mathematical_views.model: Preview reuse and cancellation transition system
mathematical_views.question: When can a preview be reused and what changes when navigation selects a replacement?
assumptions: Model preview state using the selected URL, file characteristics, skip offset, optional lock, cancellation token, and directory-loader handle
Unchanged means the implementation's characteristic comparison succeeds, not that bytes are globally immutable
Cancellation requests stop obsolete work through the inspected hooks and select boundary; this abstraction does not prove all external processes stop immediately

costs: Queue growth and cancellation bookkeeping under load

benefits: Reuse and incremental updates reduce repeated work
costs: Freshness and lifecycle coordination depend on metadata and cancellation
Serialization constraints and synchronous application callbacks

evidence.title: Yazi v0.3.3 README
evidence.notes: Official project identity and advertised asynchronous scheduling and Lua plugin architecture. Ref v0.3.3 resolved using the official repository commit API; implementation claims below use pinned source rather than performance marketing.

evidence.title: Scheduler queues, cancellation, workers, and progress
evidence.notes: Inspected Scheduler fields, serve, cancel, and schedule_micro/schedule_macro (lines 366-416). Both priority queues and the progress channel are unbounded; macro dispatch checks ongoing task identity.

evidence.title: Tab preview lifecycle
evidence.notes: Inspected Preview::go, go_folder, abort, reset, and content_unchanged. Directory stream chunks use an entry cap and timeout and emit prepared tickets.

evidence.title: Asynchronous and synchronous Lua peek
evidence.notes: Inspected spawn_blocking, slim_lua, instruction cancellation hooks, select, and application-layer synchronous callback.

evidence.title: Lua synchronization bridge
evidence.notes: Inspected sync_isolate and retrieve: sendable argument/result conversion, application callback, and one-shot response. This is a state coordination boundary, not evidence of hostile-plugin isolation.
